coherence.reasons: Both run the same diagnosis-to-plan logic from the same margin bridge, and in both the five moves sum to the stated margin (X: $29.6M to 3.2% on $1,412M; Y: $27.4M to 3.02% on $1,414.5M). X is tighter, but two of its five moves hang loosely: private label (0.27 pp) has no supporting page, and the $3.5M shrink gain inside 'store hours' is never derived. Its headline 3.2% is also stated before a wage rise that X itself says leaves about 2.7%. Y opens with the three tests (the $29.8M gap, the $4.7M covenant need, the $25M cap), sizes every move in its own section, and backs the bridge with appendix reconciliations. Y's weak spots are that it counts all nine store exits in the 3.0% while calling three of them 'decide on evidence', and that its 3.0% is also before the wage rise.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred type of plan: reprice delivery, prune losing promotions, fix shrink, grow private label, exit weak stores at lease expiry, and avoid an across-the-board hours cut. Y weighs trade-offs better. It confines promotion cuts to stores outside ValuMart areas and names ValuMart as the highest risk with an early signal and response. It defers the three costly exits on a 3.4-year payback until the first six show the real transfer rate. It holds the cut in best-staffed stores as a reserve until shrink holds, and builds $6.5M of reserves against the wage rise, admitting the result is 2.96%. It also rules out overhead cuts, a shelf-price rise and closing delivery with reasons. X includes a targeted trim of the best-staffed quarter in its base case, which is defensible, and fairly says both plans can meet the covenant. But X leaves the wage rise as an unmitigated risk that drops the plan to about 2.7%, below target, and considers fewer alternatives.

evidence.reasons: The core numbers are right in both: the bridge, the $10.4M e-commerce drag, the $3.0M fulfillment saving from the fee test, $6.6M from store exits, and per-order losses. Y uses more of the critical evidence: the explicit $29.8M target gap, the e-commerce team's 6.1% as about $7.8M, a 71% break-even share of new sales, the $11.6M of wage cost absorbed by fewer hours, shrink composition, and a year-by-year rebuild of fulfillment cost. Y also flags that attributing all the shrink rise to hours is an upper bound because theft is 35% of shrink, and notes that the pack does not say how many stores sit near a ValuMart. Its rebuttal of the category team covers both sales-versus-profit and the lack of like-for-like store comparison; X covers only the first. X calls its $7.5M shrink offset 'cautious' although it makes the same full-attribution assumption, and its $3.5M shrink gain is unexplained. Y's flaws are that it uses the upper-bound $10.05M offset to assert the draft 'misses $20M', and that reaching 2.3% fleet shrink with flat hours is optimistic, though labelled a planning choice.

revision.reasons: Both revise management's hypothesis correctly and for the right reasons: labor is 13% of the fall, the 9.4% wage rise was largely absorbed by a 6% fall in hours per $1,000 of sales, and low-labor stores have the highest shrink. Both grant that wage inflation is real and carry the 2027 rise forward as a risk. Both reject the e-commerce freeze because it leaves a $10.4M loss in place. X keeps the supportable part of the hypothesis as a targeted trim in the best-staffed quarter and fairly notes the draft could meet the covenant. Y quantifies the absorbed wage cost ($11.6M), keeps the same targeted cut as a conditional reserve, and frames wages as 'a headwind to manage, not the cause to fix first'. Y's claim that the draft misses the covenant leans on an upper-bound assumption, which offsets its fuller treatment.

overall.reasons: Both documents get the diagnosis right, reject the draft plan on quantified grounds, and present a sized plan that reaches about 3.0% within the capital cap with the covenant in view. Y serves the CEO better for a board decision. It sets out the three tests the plan must pass, sizes every move transparently, and separates planning choices from pack inputs. It localises promotion cuts away from ValuMart areas and stages the three costly store exits. It also gives a risk table with early signals and a sized reserve against the 2027 wage rise, while admitting the plan then lands just under target. X is more concise and more even-handed on the draft plan's covenant position. But it leaves the wage rise unmitigated at about 2.7%, has two thinly supported moves (private label and the shrink gain), and weighs fewer alternatives.
